title: Maritime NDT & Class Audit Support | Ingleside, Texas
description: Level III audit prep for Ingleside fabricators, NDT subcontractors and gauging firms: class, offshore, LNG module and owner audits. Send your audit scope.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting & Class Audit Support in Ingleside
html:
Ingleside fabricates steel that ends up offshore, on LNG trains and, if current plans hold, on new ships. This page is for the fabrication yards, NDT subcontractors and gauging companies around Ingleside and Corpus Christi Bay that must pass a certification body, class society or owner audit of their NDT. As an ASNT NDT Level III consulting firm, Atlantis gets your written practice, procedures and personnel records ready for the audit, rehearses it with you, and helps you close whatever the auditor raises. Name the audit you are facing and we will outline what the work involves.

What gets built and loaded on the Ingleside waterfront

The center of gravity is fabrication. Kiewit Offshore Services built its yard on Corpus Christi Bay in 2001 and has used it for offshore and onshore modules ever since; trade press credits the yard with the offshore substation for the South Fork Wind project. In 2026 Glenfarne selected Kiewit Offshore Services to fabricate the liquefaction, pretreatment and pipe rack modules for its Texas LNG export project in Brownsville at the Ingleside yard, on notice to proceed. Module work of that kind lives under process piping and pressure vessel codes, not ship rules, and it brings its own audit trail.

Shipbuilding may be next. In October 2026, HD Hyundai USA and Kiewit Maritime announced plans for a joint venture, HD Kiewit Shipbuilding, to develop a new shipyard in Ingleside. The partners said the venture would first look at naval auxiliary craft and commercial vessels, and at blocks and modules for other US builders, with construction targeted to start in 2027 and full operations in 2029. Until that yard exists it is a plan, not a customer, but suppliers that want its work should know that ship construction brings class rules and, for naval auxiliaries, government technical requirements as well.

Ingleside also sits on a crude oil export channel. Tankers load at the waterfront terminal and pass in and out of Corpus Christi Bay, and the thickness surveys on those ships, when they feed a class survey, belong to firms that hold approval from the ship's class society. So in one small town an NDT company can be asked to prove itself to an offshore certification body, a module owner's quality team, a class approval auditor and a tanker manager, sometimes in the same quarter.

Three audit families an Ingleside NDT program has to satisfy

Audit familyTypical triggerDocuments the auditor works fromMost common NDT gap we find
Owner and certification-body audits of fabrication NDTA new offshore structure, wind substation or LNG module contractProject specification, the structural or piping code it names, and the owner's NDT and personnel requirementsProcedures written to the code in general rather than to the project's acceptance criteria and joint types
Class society approval of service suppliersA firm wanting to gauge ships for class surveys, or to perform NDT that a society will credit on an offshore unitIACS UR Z17 and the society's own schemeOperator records that show certificates but not supervised field experience
Owner, charterer and vetting audits of gauging firmsA tanker or barge operator adding a new thickness measurement contractorThe operator's supplier questionnaire and specificationReport formats that do not identify reading locations clearly enough to repeat them

The documents overlap more than the auditors' titles suggest. All three want to see a written practice that controls who may test and sign, procedures that match the job, calibrated equipment and records that link a result to a person and an instrument. What changes is the acceptance standard, the extent of testing and the format of the report. Building those differences into job-level technique sheets, rather than into separate manuals for each customer, keeps a small firm's paperwork manageable.

Offshore structures and wind substations: who checks the NDT

Steel for offshore platforms and substations is usually welded to a structural code named in the project specification, commonly AWS D1.1 for the welding and inspection rules, with the owner's own specification adding extent of testing and acceptance criteria for critical joints. On top of that, a certification body or class society often reviews the fabrication on the owner's behalf, and offshore wind projects on the US outer continental shelf also involve the independent certified verification agent that federal rules call for. Each of those parties can ask to see your NDT records, and each can stop work if they do not like what they see.

The NDT questions they ask are predictable. Is the UT technique on heavy nodes and thick tubular joints written for the actual geometry, or borrowed from plate work? Do the technicians hold certification in the method and level the specification calls for, and does the written practice behind that certification follow the scheme the contract names, typically SNT-TC-1A or CP-189? Were MT and visual inspections done at the hold points the inspection and test plan sets, with records to prove it? Atlantis writes and reviews the UT and MT procedures and technique sheets that answer those questions; see NDT procedure development. Our pages on offshore Level III audit support and US offshore wind NDT consulting go further into those projects.

Where a project would normally call for radiography, ultrasonic examination is often accepted in its place for thick sections, if the code and owner allow it. That substitution only holds up at audit if the UT procedure has been qualified for it. Atlantis does not carry out radiography anywhere in the United States; when an Ingleside yard uses a licensed radiography subcontractor, our Level III can review the radiographs and the RT procedure as part of the yard's subcontractor control.

LNG modules: piping and vessel NDT under ASME codes

A liquefaction or pretreatment module is mostly process piping and pressure equipment on a steel frame. The piping NDT follows ASME B31.3 and the owner's specification; the vessels follow ASME Section VIII; the frame follows the structural code. Each code names different examination extents and acceptance criteria, and module owners frequently tighten them. B31.3 leaves the qualification of examination personnel to the employer's written practice, which is why owners audit that document closely, and many require the scheme behind it to be SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 by name. Our ASME B31.3 page explains the examination categories that drive the extent of testing.

The module audits we prepare yards for tend to focus on four things. The traceability from weld number to NDT report, because a module may carry thousands of welds and the owner will sample them. The control of examination extent when random sampling is specified, including what happens when a sample fails and progressive examination is triggered. The qualification of any advanced UT used on piping welds. And the handling of repairs, so that a repaired weld is re-examined and the record shows it. Our LNG Level III audit support and LNG written practice pages describe those programs in more depth.

One boundary to state clearly: the welding procedures and welder qualifications on a module belong to the fabricator, whose welding engineer owns them. We do not draft or qualify welding procedures. Our work starts where the weld is finished and needs to be examined, recorded and accepted.

Class approval for offshore NDT and for gauging tankers

Two different class approvals matter around Ingleside. The first is thickness measurement on ships, which IACS UR Z17 makes non-optional when a class surveyor relies on the readings. Tankers calling at the Ingleside terminal that are due for an enhanced survey need gauging by a firm that holds approval from their own society, and that approval is renewed at intervals of three years or less. The second is NDT on offshore units and projects, which some societies also approve under their service supplier schemes; DNV, for example, issues offshore NDT approvals under its class programmes. Each society runs its own version of the process and issues its own certificate. Our pages on DNV service supplier approval and the IACS service supplier requirements set out the detail.

Firms applying from the Texas coast often stumble on the same two points. First, the practical demonstration: the society wants to watch the firm perform the actual service and produce a report, and an operator who has only gauged storage tanks or pipe may not know how a ship's thickness report is laid out by structural member. Second, the supervisor: UR Z17 expects a named supervisor with real experience in the activity, and a small firm sometimes names its owner, who has not been in a tank in years. We help you choose and prepare the right people, and the ultrasonic thickness measurement page explains how ship gauging differs from plant work.

If a shipyard comes to Ingleside

A new yard building naval auxiliaries and commercial vessels would change the local NDT market. Commercial hulls are built under class rules, with hull weld NDT planned and witnessed by the society's surveyors. Naval auxiliary programs often combine class rules with Navy technical requirements, and once a contract calls up NAVSEA technical publications, that portion of the NDT falls under NAVSEA instead of the society. NAVSEA's NDT publication turns SNT-TC-1A into mandatory minimums, shortens recertification to three years for operators and inspectors, and requires procedures to be qualified within the activity that uses them.

Suppliers who want to make blocks, modules or outfitting for such a yard do not need to wait for its first contract to get ready. A written practice that already meets the stricter of the likely requirements, procedures that can be qualified quickly, and personnel files with complete training and experience evidence are what a new shipbuilder's supplier quality team will look for. Our NAVSEA shipyard requirements page lays out the differences from commercial practice.

How we work with firms around Corpus Christi Bay

Atlantis does not have an office in the Coastal Bend. Ingleside is within driving distance of Houston, so site visits are straightforward, and most of the document work is done remotely. A typical engagement for an Ingleside fabricator or NDT subcontractor looks like this:

  • Requirement read-through: we go through the project specification or the society's checklist with your QA lead and list every NDT obligation it creates.
  • Document gap review: our Level III compares your written practice, procedures, technique sheets and record templates against that list and marks each gap by the risk it poses at audit.
  • Drafting for your approval: we rewrite what needs rewriting. Your managers review, approve and sign, and the documents become yours.
  • Evidence clean-up: we help gather the training, experience, examination and vision evidence that personnel files are missing, and rebuild equipment calibration logs where they have gaps.
  • Mock audit and procedure demonstration: on site, we audit you the way the owner or society will, and witness or run procedure demonstrations where the code or project requires them.
  • Response support: once the auditor has issued findings, we help draft corrective actions that show cause, fix and evidence.

Responsibility does not move to us. Your company certifies its personnel under its written practice, the owner or certification body accepts or rejects your work, and the class society decides on approval. Our job is to make sure your documents and records give them nothing to stumble over. For broader Level III work in the Coastal Bend, see the Ingleside consulting page and the Corpus Christi Level III of record page.

Atlantis's own UR Z17 position

We are candid about this because Ingleside firms ask. Atlantis is in the middle of its own IACS UR Z17 approval process with Lloyd's Register, ABS and DNV, and today it holds no class approval from any society. The practical effect is twofold. We know the current audit process from the applicant's side, not just from reading the requirement. And we cannot offer class-credited thickness measurement until a society certifies us, so for now our maritime work is advisory: preparing your firm, your documents and your people.

What to send before we scope the work

  • The audit or contract that triggers the work: the project specification section on NDT, the society's application checklist, or the operator's supplier questionnaire.
  • Your written practice and the methods and levels you certify under it.
  • Procedures and technique sheets for the work in question, including any UT used in place of radiography.
  • Three personnel files and your current equipment and calibration list.
  • Recent reports from similar work, and any previous audit findings.

We reply within one business day. If your technicians need method training to fill a gap the audit exposes, see our maritime NDT training and refining NDT training for Ingleside.

An Ingleside audit-readiness checklist

  1. Identify which audit family each upcoming contract belongs to: owner or certification body, class approval, or operator vetting.
  2. Confirm the scheme your written practice follows matches what each contract names, and that it covers every method you will use.
  3. Check that UT procedures for thick nodes, tubulars and piping welds are written for the real geometry and qualified where the code requires it.
  4. Verify the traceability from weld number to report on a sample of recent jobs, including repaired welds.
  5. For class gauging, list the societies you hold approval from, the expiry dates, and the named supervisor for each.
  6. Review files for every NDT subcontractor you use, including any licensed radiography firm.
  7. Bring vision, calibration and certification dates current before the auditor arrives.
  8. Close open corrective actions with evidence, not promises.

For the national view, see maritime NDT audit support. Other Texas Gulf ports have their own pages for Brownsville and Houston, and the Corpus Christi area's marine industry is described on our Corpus Christi marine NDT page.

faq.q: Which audit applies to NDT on an offshore wind substation built in Ingleside?
faq.a: Usually several at once. The owner audits against its project specification, a certification body or class society may review fabrication on the owner's behalf, and offshore wind projects on the outer continental shelf involve an independent certified verification agent. All of them look at the same NDT evidence: the written practice, procedures, personnel certification and records.

faq.q: Does a gauging firm need class approval to measure tankers at the Ingleside terminal?
faq.a: If the readings support a class survey, yes, from that tanker's own class society under IACS UR Z17, renewed at intervals of no more than three years. Measurements done only for the operator's own records do not need class approval, but operators often prefer an approved firm. See UR Z17 audit preparation.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on module piping welds?
faq.a: Often, where ASME B31.3, the owner's specification and the engineering design allow it, and only with a UT procedure qualified for the purpose. The audit question is not whether UT can do the job in principle but whether your procedure and personnel are qualified for this joint and thickness.

faq.q: Will Atlantis act as the Level III for our written practice?
faq.a: We can draft the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations as your outside Level III in the methods our Level III holds: UT, RT, MT, PT and VT under ASNT. Your company remains the employer that certifies the technicians and owns the records.

faq.q: Is the new Ingleside shipyard already taking suppliers?
faq.a: As of the October 2026 announcement it was a plan, with construction targeted for 2027 and full operations for 2029. We cannot speak for the venture's supplier process. What we can do is help a fabricator or NDT firm build a program that would stand up to a shipbuilder's supplier audit when that process opens.

faq.q: Does Navy auxiliary work follow class rules or Navy rules?
faq.a: It depends on the contract. Auxiliary programs often use class rules for much of the ship and Navy technical requirements for specified systems. Where the contract invokes NAVSEA technical publications for NDT, NAVSEA rules govern that work, not the class society's.

faq.q: Do you send people to Ingleside?
faq.a: Yes, for mock audits, procedure demonstrations and floor observations. Atlantis has no office in the Coastal Bend; we travel from Houston and do the document work remotely.

faq.q: Can you take on the radiography for our project?
faq.a: No. Radiography is not something Atlantis performs in the US. If your project uses RT, you engage a licensed radiography firm; our Level III can review its procedure, film or digital images and personnel records as part of your subcontractor approval.

faq.q: Does Atlantis hold DNV, ABS or Lloyd's Register approval?
faq.a: No, not at present. Atlantis is working through UR Z17 approval with all three societies for its own thickness measurement services. Until a certificate is issued, we offer advisory support only for class-related work.

faq.q: What does an owner usually reject in a module fabricator's NDT records?
faq.a: Reports that cannot be traced to a specific weld, missing re-examination records for repaired welds, random-sampling records that do not show how failed samples were expanded, and technician certifications under a written practice that does not match the scheme the specification names. Our audit documentation work targets exactly these.
